abstract: |
  Scientific collaboration, often measured through co-authorship, has grown in many disciplines and is frequently linked to increased citation rates. However, it remains unclear which disciplines have seen the greatest growth in collaboration and how this growth relates to article-level metrics. Moreover, little is known about how team demographics (e.g., *h*-index, gender, number of institutions) and team size interact with regard to research impact. Understanding these dynamics is essential given their influence on hiring, tenure, and the broader scientific ecosystem. Using metadata from Elsevier’s International Center for the Study of Research (ICSR) Lab, we examined collaboration trends across disciplines and their associations with citation outcomes. Team size increased over time, with variation by discipline, and was positively associated with citation counts. Gender relationships with citation rates varied by authorship order and discipline, indicating a complex relationship between gender and impact. Greater institutional and geographic diversity were linked to higher citation counts. Last authors’ *h*-indices were especially strongly associated with impact, particularly when self-citations were excluded. Effect sizes were small, and the observational design precludes causal conclusions. These findings describe how evolving patterns of collaboration are related to research visibility and underscore the importance of considering team composition, cautiously, in evaluations of scientific output.

The number of co-authors on a project (i.e., team size, proxied here by
the length of the authorship list) has been increasing in many fields of
study, such as biomedical sciences [@papatheodorou2008],
medicine [@weeks2004], and psychology [@zafrunnishan.reddyv.p.2010].
Notably, the number of co-authors is one factor that may be positively
associated with article metrics [e.g., citation rates, @larivière2015;
@wuchty2007], although the extent of this relationship may vary by field
[e.g., physics, @hinnant2012]. Within co-authored papers, additional
characteristics of the authorship team may be related to these metrics.
Author diversity, broadly speaking, has been associated with
positive outcomes such as publication in high-impact factor journals,
rates of citations, and funding [@freeman2015; @nichols2014]. It is
important to note that author diversity can be conceptualized along a
continuum of factors such as gender, physical location (e.g., United
States, Brazil), institutional affiliation, discipline, and rank.
Evidence suggests the impact of international collaboration, rank, and
gender on article metrics in fields such as sport science
research [@wang2015], physics [@hinnant2012], and psychology [@geraci2015],
respectively. Despite the benefits of having diversity among co-authors
for scientific productivity and impact, co-author teams tend to be
homogenous [TODO: add citation; Kelly's note points to
PMC6703830]. For example, when looking at gender, authors exhibit a
tendency to work with others of the same gender, a finding that is
stable over time [TODO: add citation; Kelly's note points to
Scientometrics s11192-023-04885-1]. Thus, recommendations for scientists
to increase co-author representation [TODO: add citation; Kelly's note
points to a Drive PDF] may not be effective without careful
consideration about team composition.

The available research paints an incomplete picture of co-authorship
trends and their relationship to citation metrics. Landmark studies have
documented the growth of team size and its association with citations
over long time spans [e.g., 1900--2011, @larivière2015; 1955--2000,
@wuchty2007], and the gender gap in authorship has been studied across
countries, disciplines, and career stages [@lariviere2013; @huang2020].
However, these literatures have largely developed separately, and less
is known about how team size and several features of team composition
(gender, the *h*-index of the first and last authors, and the number of
institutions and countries represented) are jointly related to
article-level citation metrics within and across disciplines in a
single, contemporary, article-level dataset. Subsequently, understanding
co-author team composition is critical given previous research showing
that, despite the benefits of co-authorship diversity, people tend to
work with those similar to them. As such, this project aims to first
establish trends in co-authorship team size within disciplines across
time and then explore how the composition of these co-authorship teams
is related to citation metrics. The research questions guiding these
aims are as follows: 1a.) What is the pattern of team size distribution
within various disciplines over time, 1b.) is team size related to
article impact?, and 2.) What characteristics of team composition have
the strongest association with article metrics?

## *Question 1*. What is the pattern of team size distribution within various disciplines over time, and is team size related to article impact?

Initiatives, calls, and funding opportunities for collaborative research
(from both private and public/government sectors) have been increasing in
recent years, with some arguing that large teams (i.e., co-authors) are
necessary for addressing modern societal questions and
problems [@samarasekera2009]. Concurrently, various disciplines have
reported changes in co-authorship trends [@papatheodorou2008; @wuchty2007].
Discipline-specific investigations have identified co-authorship trends
that differ by subdiscipline. For example, over the last approximately 30
years co-authorship has doubled in subfields of the natural/physical
sciences like physics and musculoskeletal science [@russell2019], while
growth in mathematics has been notably slower [@grossman2002]. Among the
social sciences, a more consistent pattern of increased co-authorship
emerged, although specific changes vary by subfield [@hunter2008;
@kozlowski2017; @demeuse2014; @rath2016; @gaunt2014]. This suggests that
needs and norms within various disciplines may influence how quickly and
to what extent authorship trends change and solidify. Because the current
state of the research focuses on constructs like time [@abu2019],
disciplinary journal [@demeuse2014], and geographical region [@leifeld2017]
in isolation, examining co-authorship trends among multiple disciplines
concurrently would afford a more holistic overview of the state of team
science.

Examining co-authorship trends across time and disciplines alongside
citation metrics will also facilitate a deeper understanding of the
conditions under which co-authorship is associated with impact. For
example, among publications indexed in the annual volumes of the Web of
Knowledge™ in 2007, single-author papers received an average of 2.91
citations while multi-author papers exhibited an average of
5.39 [@thijs2015]; this difference was consistent when examining citation
averages from 1998 to 2007. Further probing this relationship, it appears
that the number of citations increases with the number of authors, up to
a point (approx. 20 authors) after which the relationship becomes
inconsistent. This non-linear relationship between team size and impact
suggests that other factors, such as the composition of the team, may
contribute to the observed benefits when co-authored teams come together.
We emphasize that team size is treated here as a descriptive feature of
the authorship list; our analyses are observational and cannot establish
that adding authors causes higher impact.

## *Question 2*. What characteristics of team composition have the strongest association with article metrics?

When thinking about the composition of organizations, including teams,
scholars have documented both positive and negative effects of
diversity [TODO: add citation]. On the one hand, through team diversity
members gain more insight about the task through varied perspectives. On
the other hand, dissimilarities can create tension [TODO: add citation].
The extent to which teams take advantage of the diversity of their
members through discussion and the exchange of information may depend on
characteristics of individual members that facilitate either
open-mindedness or social categorization and intergroup bias
[TODO: add citation]. Simulation research has also noted that the effect
of diversity on team performance follows a curvilinear relationship with
performance [TODO: add citation; Kelly's note points to
jasss.org/9/3/3.html]. The Categorization--Elaboration Model
[CEM, @vanknippenberg2004] integrates these perspectives: diversity
(whether based on social categories or on differences in information and
expertise) can stimulate the elaboration of task-relevant information,
which benefits performance, but categorization processes can undermine
that benefit.

The CEM provides a conceptual rationale for examining the present
variables together. Gender is a social-category characteristic of the
team; the number of institutions and countries represented index
affiliation-based (and likely information-based) diversity; and the
*h*-index of the first and last authors indexes the status and expertise
that authors bring to the team. Team size sets the number of people among
whom these differences can be distributed, and is therefore both a
covariate for and a context of the composition variables (indeed,
institution and country counts cannot exceed team size). We selected these
variables because they are the author-level characteristics available at
scale in the Scopus metadata, and we treat them as correlates of citation
metrics rather than as causal mechanisms. This research on team diversity
must also be considered alongside sociocultural research about how members
of certain groups have historically been treated in the sciences.

Generally speaking, despite increases in
women's representation in academia, women still are underrepresented
when it comes to publishing co- and solo-authored papers [@jagsi2006]. In
addition to authoring a smaller proportion of published work, research
suggests women are also less likely to hold prominent authorship
positions [@west2013; @rigg2012]. For example, women are underrepresented
regarding publishing articles in specific areas of
medicine [@süßenbacher2017; @cushman2022], STEM fields [e.g.,
mathematics, @mihaljevic-brandt2016], and social
sciences [@mihaljevic-brandt2016; @bonham2017], although the extent of
these differences vary by subfield [e.g., computational biology, as
compared to biology in general, @bonham2017]. Interestingly, women are
less likely to collaborate with previous co-authors compared to
men [@zeng2016]; although it is not clear why this is the case, it could
have important implications for their careers as novel teams tend to
produce higher-impact work [@katzenbach2003].

Furthermore, women are less likely to receive credit for their
contributions to empirical and scholarly work [@ross2022]. A growing body
of research suggests that contributions by women to peer-reviewed
publications are often perceived as less valuable than those authored by
men. After controlling for the year of publication, publication outlet,
focus, theoretical framework, methodology, tenure status, and
institutional affiliation, women were still cited less than
men [@maliniak2013]. Relevant to this manuscript is the body of research
examining the association between gender and citation rates. Previous
work has noted that in specific fields, men are less likely to cite
women's work and work authored by women typically receives fewer
citations overall [@cameron2016; @hutson2002]. This difference in the
likelihood of accumulating citations could influence a researchers'
impact [@rezek2011], which is often considered important for career
advances.

One commonly used measure of a scholar's output and impact is the
"*h*-index" [@hirsch2005]. The *h*-index combines the number of articles
published with the number of citations received for those articles. This
approach attempts to balance high-impact articles with the number of
articles published. Specifically, the *h*-score is the number of
articles (X) that receive X citations. The *h*-index is one of the most
widely used measures of a scholar's impact [@crespo2019], although it
has also been criticized, for example for its dependence on field and
career length and for behaving inconsistently when comparing
scholars [@bornmann2007; @waltman2012].
Fields such as psychology have observed gender differences pertaining to
*h*-indices that favor men. Women professors have a significantly lower
*h*-index than men, with a difference of approximately four points.
After controlling for the year of first publication, gender shares
approximately 2.6% of the variance with *h*-index [@geraci2015]. This
effect was examined relative to mean salaries for full professors, and
practically translated to an astounding effect of \$13,100 a year
difference between men and women [@geraci2015].

Notable is that the calculation of *h*-indices may be particularly
biased by self-citations and years without publication. Higher rates of
citations received by men were partially explained by high rates of
self-citation which altered scores up to 14 extra *h*-index points.
Women also engaged in self-citation, although less so, and only
impacting their *h*-index by up to 5 points [@cameron2016]. It is
important to note that there is evidence of increasing equity between
genders in certain fields; in international relations, for example, the
gap between men's and women's manuscript submissions and publications
are narrowing, and there appears to be no significant relationship
between gender and citation count [@østby2013]. Although there are
alternatives to the *h*-index that account for self-citations [e.g., the
*b*-index, @brown2009], the *h*-index remains popular, and we use it here
as one available (and imperfect) indicator of an author's prior
visibility rather than as a measure of scholarly quality.

Given the arguments regarding the necessity of scientific collaboration
and large international teams to address modern societal questions and
problems [@samarasekera2009], it may be intuitive that institutional and
geographical diversity is on the rise. One source notes an increase in
Psychology articles that have the presence of both a U.S. author and at
least one international co-author [@kliegl2011]. Similar increases in
the fraction of internationally co-authored papers (i.e., ratio of
co-authored articles with international institutions to the total number
of co-authored articles with domestic and international institutions)
were noted in other scientific disciplines, such as mathematics,
biology, medicine, and engineering [@coccia2016]. However, while it
appears most fields are increasing international engagement, applied
fields (especially medical sciences) have higher rates of
growth [@coccia2016a].

Collaboration involving those outside of one's home institution and
country may significantly impact article metrics, which may be one
reason for the increasing rates of international collaboration. For
instance, for UK institutions indexed in the Science Citation Index
between 1981 and 1994, collaboration within one's home university or
country resulted in a small increase in average impact (0.75 citations)
whereas collaboration outside of one's home country resulted in a more
moderate increase [1.6 citations, @katz1997]. Indeed, both
well-established and young institutions benefit from international
collaboration as evidenced by a citation per paper increase when the
authorship team is international [@khor2016]. This benefit is
corroborated by the observation that international co-authorship
publications are over-represented in the ESI global top 10 % highly
cited publications relative to all journal publications from the same
institution [@khor2016]. Indeed, article impact in terms of citations per
paper seems to be greatest for those manuscripts with multiple domestic
and international collaborators, and the smallest for those with no
institutional collaboration.

However, this trend may not be consistent across fields, journals,
and/or countries, and warrants further investigation [e.g.,
physics, @hinnant2012; @rousseau2016]. For example, international
collaboration generally increases citation rates in the field of sports
science, but the extent of this effect varies by which countries are
collaborating [@wang2015]. Collaboration between the United States and
Canada, for instance, produced a mean citation rate greater than the
domestic mean observed citation rate of each country respectively,
whereas collaboration between the United Kingdom and Greece produced a
mean citation rate that was lower than the domestic mean observed
citation rate of each country respectively. Furthermore, when examining
the benefits of international collaboration on citation count for
American authors publishing in the top three interdisciplinary journals
(*Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* [PNAS], *Nature*, and
*Science*), there is an increased citation rate for international
collaboration when compared to American-only authored
papers [@rousseau2016]. It is important to note that this effect was the
result of a significant increase in citation rate for international
papers published in *PNAS* only. When examining each journal
independently, no benefit of international collaboration was found for
*Science* or *Nature*. Given the accelerated growth of international
collaboration across various fields over time [@coccia2016a; @walsh2007],
it is increasingly important to understand the influence of this
diversity on article metrics.

The majority of work examining team characteristics and article metrics
have focused on a specific field [@hinnant2012], and/or a
limited/restricted number of team characteristics [e.g.,
size, @wuchty2007]. Empirical data comparing the impact of
diverse/multiple team characteristics on article metrics within a given
field is limited [@weeks2004; @hinnant2012; @wang2015; @grossman2002;
@nabout2015]. Along a similar vein, empirical data comparing the impact
of team characteristics on article metrics across fields is also limited
[for notable exceptions, @larivière2015; @wuchty2007]. 
Comparing outcomes within and across fields can
allow for an increased understanding of these fields' scientific
culture. Practically, understanding factors associated with an article's
impact can be important for researchers' outreach, as well as planning
for the job market and tenure review.

# Method

## Ethics Information

All of the data for this manuscript is drawn from peer-reviewed
journals. All of the extracted meta-data from the individual
publications are de-identified in the database. As such, per US Federal
Guidelines, this research is not subject to human ethics review boards
(§46.101, (b) (4)).

## Design

This study was an archival data investigation into scholarly publication
records using Elsevier's curated database Scopus. This study was
conducted through access to Elsevier's International Center for the
Study of Research Lab (ICSR; <https://www.elsevier.com/icsr>). The ICSR
is designed to support researchers in their empirical study of
meta-science on large datasets using the Databricks platform running
Apache Spark architecture for big-data analyses. Through ICSR,
researchers can access full publication metadata from Scopus including
article metrics, author(s), and affiliation information. The data
snapshot used was ICSR version v008 (snapshot dated 9 May 2023), and all
citation counts reflect citations accrued up to that date. The unit of analysis was the journal article.
For each article, we used the publication year, the ordered list of
authors (and each author's inferred gender, *h*-index, and
affiliations), the journal's ASJC subject classification, and citation
counts. Scopus contains over 80 million entries from 1788 to present
[@boyle2006]; we restricted the data as described in the Sampling Plan
below. All variables extracted from this dataset are described below.

### Variables

Article characteristics included the year of publication, number of
authors (team size), and discipline. Team size was operationalized as
the number of authors on the article's authorship list; this is a common
proxy for the size of the team that produced the work, but it is not
strictly synonymous with it (e.g., it excludes acknowledged contributors).
Discipline was defined using the All Science Journal Classification
(ASJC;
<https://service.elsevier.com/app/answers/detail/a_id/15181/supporthub/scopus/>)
with the five global subject area codes (Health, Physical, Life, Social
Sciences, and Multidisciplinary).[^1] Because the ASJC is assigned at the
level of the journal, an article takes the classification of the journal
in which it was published. The Multidisciplinary category therefore
reflects the type of journal (e.g., broad-scope outlets) and not the
disciplinary makeup of the author team. Journals
carrying more than one ASJC code were counted in each of the corresponding
areas, so an article could contribute to more than one subject-area
model; the overall models counted each article once. Articles whose
journals fell outside the four named areas were classified as
Multidisciplinary. Metric characteristics included citation count
(the number of times an article was cited within the current data
snapshot, including self-citations) and five-year citation count (the
number of citations received within five years of publication, as
supplied in the ICSR field-weighted citation impact table; this is the raw
count, not the field-normalized ratio). For the five-year citation models we included only articles published
before 2017, so that every article had a complete five-year window.

[^1]: We originally planned on using the 27 subfields within the ASJC.
    However, we updated our preregistration to use only five of the
    larger subfields due to computational constraints.

Author characteristics included affiliation country,
affiliation/institution, *h*-index, gender, and gender ratio. We
transformed affiliation countries into a count variable of the number of
unique countries. Similarly, we transformed affiliation/institutions
into a count of the number of different affiliations across authors. We
used the *h*-index of the first and last authors for each article, with
and without self-citation. Author position was used as recorded; we did
not assume that the last author is the most senior member of the team
(see Limitations). Last, Elsevier has noted that their inferred
gender column has a 97% accuracy, and we used the inferred gender of the
first and last authors for each article. From this variable, we
additionally calculated the gender ratio (number of inferred male /
total authors) as a single variable for each article.

### Sampling Plan

While Scopus includes articles from 1788 to present, we limited our
sample to journal articles published from 1970 until the date of the data
snapshot. Scopus indicates that articles from 1970 to present include
reference information, which was required to calculate several of the
above mentioned variables. We originally planned to include all eligible
articles from 1970 forward. Due to computational constraints, we randomly
sampled 25% of eligible articles during this time span to constrain the
run time of our code and the memory necessary to calculate *h*-index.
Articles were
sampled by simple random sampling (fixed seed), so the sample is expected
to be representative of the eligible population, and with several million
articles per subject area the sampling error is negligible. However, we
did not compare the sample with the full population, nor repeat the
sampling, so we cannot demonstrate representativeness across publication
years or subject areas; this is a limitation. It is important to note that we did *not* calculate *h*-index on
the randomly sampled dataset. These values were calculated on the full
data and then merged with the randomly sampled data to ensure
*h*-indices were appropriate for authors on the randomly sampled data.

### Power

Given the large size of the Scopus dataset, all analyses were expected to
achieve the required 95% power. Analyses using the *pwr*
library [@champely2017] indicated that the planned regressions had the
ability to detect effects at $R^2$ \< .00001 at 95% power using a 95%
confidence interval. Because such tiny effects are detectable, statistical
significance is uninformative here; we therefore emphasize the magnitude
of the effects (the slopes and $R^2$) when interpreting the results.

```{r power-analysis, echo = F, include = F, eval = F}
pwr.f2.test(u = 1, #df num
            v = (DF %>% filter(subjareas != "undefined") %>% pull(sample) %>% min)*100, #df denom
            f2 = NULL, 
            sig.level = 0.05, 
            power = .95)
pwr.f2.test(u = 2, #df num
            v = (DF %>% filter(subjareas != "undefined") %>% pull(sample) %>% min)*100, #df denom
            f2 = NULL, 
            sig.level = 0.05, 
            power = .95)
pwr.f2.test(u = 3, #df num
            v = (DF %>% filter(subjareas != "undefined") %>% pull(sample) %>% min)*100, #df denom
            f2 = NULL, 
            sig.level = 0.05, 
            power = .95)
```

## Analysis Plan

### Data Availability

While we cannot provide access to the full dataset because it is only
accessible through access granted by Elsevier, we provide our
analysis code via GitHub and the Open Science Framework. Persons
interested in replicating or extending the current work can do so
through using the ICSR lab Databricks platform. ICSR has stated to the
paper's authors that they will guarantee access to researchers who want
to follow up or reproduce our results.

### Code Availability

We were allowed to use a small subset of cases (1%) to create the
analysis code for the proposed research questions. This code and output
are available at <https://osf.io/g4qnp/> and
<https://github.com/doomlab/big_team_size>. Our study was preregistered
at <https://osf.io/j63fd>, which includes an update due to deviations
from the original plan. The code used to create this manuscript with the
*papaja* package [@aust2022] can be found online as well.

### Data Screening

Missing data was excluded for the analyses in which the data was missing
only. We assumed all data is accurate. In all analyses, we examined the
cell counts for each categorical variable to collapse small cell sizes
(i.e., *n* \< 5). No articles were considered outliers, as all
publication data was expected to be part of the population.

In each relevant analysis, we examined for multicollinearity of the IVs,
as team size may positively correlate with count variables calculated in
later research questions. If values were multicollinear, *r* \> .90, we
planned to note these correlations and only use one of the proposed
variables. No values reached this criteria for the five subject areas.
In our analyses, a linear trend was the main focus of interest, and we
did not note any non-linear trends. Nearly all scatter plots indicated
heteroscedasticity, and team size and citation counts are discrete,
non-negative, and highly right-skewed (with many uncited articles),
which are conditions under which count models (e.g., Poisson or negative
binomial, possibly zero-inflated) are often preferred. We retained
ordinary least squares linear models for three reasons: (a) they were
specified in our preregistration; (b) with samples of this size,
inference about the slopes does not depend on the normality of the
residuals; and (c) the slopes are directly interpretable as the expected
difference in citations per additional author (or per one-unit
difference in an author characteristic), which we use throughout.
However, the standard errors and confidence intervals from these models
should be interpreted cautiously given the heteroscedasticity, and the
linear models may misrepresent the conditional mean at the extremes of
the distribution. We did not run
negative binomial, zero-inflated, or other count-data models, and we no
longer have access to the data to do so; this is a limitation of the
present work. Please see Appendix A for further details.

### Decision Criteria

The large sample size was expected to indicate all predictors
significant at the traditional *p* value criterion. For individual
predictors, we used the 95% confidence intervals of the slope to
indicate if the effect was non-zero (i.e., the confidence interval did
not include zero rounded to three decimals). Because significance was
expected for even trivial effects, we interpreted the size of the slopes
and of $R^2$ rather than significance alone. The difference between
effects was determined by examining the confidence intervals of
$R^2$ to three decimal places calculated with the *MBESS* library
[@kelley2022]. If they did not overlap, we stated that they were
different.

### Research Questions

All analyses were performed using *pyspark* [@pyspark] within the
Databricks system. Visualization and presentation of analyses were
included using *R* [@R-base], *dplyr* [@R-dplyr], *rio* [@becker2021],
*tidyr* [@R-tidyr], *patchwork* [@R-patchwork], and *ggplot2* [@R-ggplot2].

*Research Question 1a: What is the pattern of team size distribution
within various disciplines over time?*

We first calculated the mean, median, and interquartile range of team
size by subject area. We did not explicitly compare discipline
intercepts in a *post hoc* format with any form of test. Instead, we
present visualizations to display the distribution and their
interquartile range for readers to examine.

In order to determine if team sizes change overall across time, we used
a linear model of team size predicted by year of publication in which
each article was only represented once, regardless of discipline. We
examined if the confidence interval of the slope parameter was different
from zero to determine if the predictor was significant. Last, we
calculated each subject area's slope and confidence interval using a
linear model of team size predicted by year of publication. Again, we
provide these slopes in a visualization for readers to examine with no
official *post hoc* comparison. A single model with discipline as a
dummy-coded factor (fully interacted with year) would return the same
discipline-specific slopes as separate models, so we estimated the
discipline models separately; a multilevel model with random effects
for discipline was not feasible because no *pyspark* multilevel model
implementation exists to model data at this scale. We did not test the
year-by-discipline interaction in a pooled model.

*Research Question 1b: Is team size related to article impact?*

For this research question, we examined the association between team size and
article publication metrics for impact. Our hypothesis was that team
size is associated with article metrics (non-directional). We ran these analyses
once for each dependent variable of citation count and five-year
citation count. We calculated the mean, median, and interquartile range
of each publication metric by discipline. We provide visualizations of
these values instead of comparing them directly.

To determine the association of team size with publication metrics, we
used a linear model of publication metrics predicted by time of
publication (covariate) and team size. Year of publication entered as a
main effect only (i.e., no team size by year interaction was modeled)
Year and team size
were entered as raw values (not centered or scaled), so only the slopes are
interpretable. We did not test a polynomial term for non-linearity.
Team size was entered as a linear term only. We included time as a
covariate, as we expected that older articles would potentially have more or different
metrics because they have been around longer to cite. We examined if the
confidence interval of the team size slope parameter was different from
zero. Last, we calculated the slope for team size for each subject area
separately. We visualized these differences and the confidence
intervals.

*Research Question 2: What characteristics of team composition have the
strongest association with article metrics?*

For this research question, we continued to use the model from the
previous research question and added other article metrics to determine
their contribution to the model. Our hypothesis was that each variable
is associated with the metrics variables (non-directional). Each author
independent variable was modeled separately and compared using confidence
intervals as described above to determine which variable had the
strongest association with publication metrics. The author variables
entered as main effects only; interactions with team size or year were
not modeled.

Using the linear model from the previous research question, we added
each author independent variable (affiliation country count,
affiliation/institution count, *h*-index, gender (male versus female),
and gender ratio) in separate models to calculate their slope. We
determined if these slopes were important by examining if their
confidence interval was greater than zero. We examined the effects of
each author metric separately. When examining first and/or last author
information, the single author paper presents a unique problem because
they are both first and last authors. Therefore, these cannot be
included in the same model. In order not to use the same variance twice,
single author papers were treated as first author only, and missing
data for last author analyses. If these were included in the same model,
all single author papers would be dropped, which would bias the results.
We then compared each overall $R^2$ to determine if their confidence
intervals overlap. This analysis was used to indicate which author
variable provided the most predictive information (since all other
covariates are the same for each analysis, only the author variable is
different). Last, we calculated each author independent variable
separated by subject area and then visualized those $R^2$ and confidence
intervals for each variable.

# Results

```{r import-data}
DF <- import(here("03_manuscript", "data", "descriptives_output_df_200723_part1.csv"))
DF2 <- bind_rows(import(here("03_manuscript", "data", 
                             "model_output_200723_part1.csv")), 
                 import(here("03_manuscript", "data", 
                             "model_output_310723_part2.csv")))
```

## Research Question 1a: What is the pattern of team size distribution within various disciplines over time?

### Descriptive Statistics

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-desc-r1) displays the mean, standard deviation,
median, and interquartile range for each subject area. The median was
generally five to six authors, except for the social sciences, which had
a median of three authors per manuscript. Mean values were generally
from four to nine authors, with the most variability in team size for
the physical sciences.

```{r fig-desc-r1, fig.cap="Boxplot of team size by subject areas. The boxplot represents the median (middle bar), the interquartile range (box), and the mean (dot) for each subject area. The plot was capped at 15 for visualization purposes. The size of the mean point represents the sample size of the number of articles used within the calculation. The size of the box represents the standard deviation of the mean for team size (i.e., larger boxes indicate more variance in the team size).", fig.height=6, fig.width=10}
hyp1a <- DF %>% filter(model == "hyp1a") %>% filter(subjareas != "undefined")
hyp1a[ , c("mean", "sd", "median", "iqr_25", "iqr_75")] <- apply(hyp1a[ , c("mean", "sd", "median", "iqr_25", "iqr_75")], 2, as.numeric)
hyp1a$sd_width <- hyp1a$sd/sum(hyp1a$sd)
ggplot(hyp1a, aes(subjareas, median)) + 
  geom_boxplot(
   aes(ymin = 1, lower = iqr_25, middle = median, 
       upper = iqr_75, ymax = 15),
   stat = "identity", width = hyp1a$sd_width) + 
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0,15)) + 
  geom_point(aes(subjareas, mean, size = sample)) + 
  theme_linedraw() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust=1), 
        legend.position = "none") + 
  xlab("Discipline Areas") + 
  ylab("Median, Mean, and IQR of Team Size") + 
  coord_flip() + 
  theme(text = element_text(size = 16))
ggsave(here("03_manuscript", "figures", "fig1-desc-r1.jpg"), width = 10, height = 6)
```

### Model Statistics

```{r hyp1a-statistics}
hyp1a_model <- DF2 %>% filter(grepl("hyp1a", model))
# add predictor information
hyp1a_model$predictor <- rep(c("team_size", "intercept"), nrow(hyp1a_model)/2)
hyp1a_model <- hyp1a_model %>% 
  filter(predictor == "team_size") %>% 
  separate(col = "model", 
           into = c("model", "subjareas"), 
           sep = "_",
           fill = "right") %>% 
  left_join(hyp1a, by = c("subjareas" = "subjareas"))
hyp1a_model$sample[is.na(hyp1a_model$subjareas)] <- sum(hyp1a_model$sample, na.rm = T)
# get CIs effects (df = N - k - 1)
hyp1a_model$critical <- qt(.05/2, hyp1a_model$sample - 2 - 1, lower.tail = F)
hyp1a_model$lower <- hyp1a_model$coef - hyp1a_model$critical*hyp1a_model$se
hyp1a_model$upper <- hyp1a_model$coef + hyp1a_model$critical*hyp1a_model$se
# get CIs R2
hyp1a_model$r2lower <- hyp1a_model$r2upper <- NA
for(i in 1:nrow(hyp1a_model)){
  temp <- ci.R2(R2 = hyp1a_model$r2[i], 
        df.1 = 1, 
        df.2 = hyp1a_model$sample[i] - 2 - 1)
  hyp1a_model$r2lower[i] <- temp$Lower.Conf.Limit.R2
  hyp1a_model$r2upper[i] <- temp$Upper.Conf.Limit.R2
}
```

The regression analysis for team size predicting year was different from
zero, *b* = `r hyp1a_model %>% filter(is.na(subjareas)) %>% pull(coef)`,
95% CI [`r hyp1a_model %>% filter(is.na(subjareas)) %>% pull(lower)`,
`r hyp1a_model %>% filter(is.na(subjareas)) %>% pull(upper)`]. This
result indicated that team size increases across time, wherein overall
team sizes are likely to increase by at least one author every 13 years.
Figure \@ref(fig:fig-heatmap) shows the results by subject area. All
subject area coefficients were greater than zero, where health and life
sciences were similar, physical sciences had the highest team size
growth, and social sciences had the lowest. The coefficients are
presented with their 95% confidence interval in Appendix A.

## Research Question 1b: Is team size related to article impact?

### Descriptive Statistics Citation Count

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-desc-r1b) displays the mean, standard deviation,
median, and interquartile range for the citation counts and five-year
citation count statistics. Multidisciplinary papers appear to have the
highest median and mean citation counts, followed by life and physical
sciences, and then social and health sciences. The pattern of results is
similar for both overall citation counts and five-year citation counts.

```{r fig-desc-r1b, fig.cap="Boxplot of citation counts by subject area. The boxplot represents the median (middle bar), the interquartile range (box), and the mean (dot) for overall citations and five year citation count. The plot was capped at 60 citations for visualization purposes. The size of the mean point represents the sample size of the number of articles used within the calculation. The size of the box represents the standard deviation of the mean for citation count (i.e., larger boxes indicate more variance in the citation counts).", fig.height=6, fig.width=10}
hyp1b <- DF %>% 
  filter(grepl("hyp1b", model)) %>% 
  filter(subjareas != "undefined") %>% 
  separate(col = model, into = c("model", "DV"), sep = "_")
hyp1b[ , c("mean", "sd", "median", "iqr_25", "iqr_75")] <- apply(hyp1b[ , c("mean", "sd", "median", "iqr_25", "iqr_75")], 2, as.numeric)
hyp1b <- hyp1b %>% 
  group_by(DV) %>% 
  mutate(sd_width = sd/sum(sd)) %>% 
  mutate(DV = factor(DV, 
                     levels = c("CitationCount", "Citation5y"),
                     labels = c("Overall Citations", "Citation 5 Years")))
ggplot(hyp1b, aes(subjareas, median)) + 
  facet_wrap(~DV) + 
  geom_boxplot(
   aes(ymin = 0, lower = iqr_25, middle = median, 
       upper = iqr_75, ymax = 60),
   stat = "identity", width = hyp1b$sd_width) + 
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) + 
  geom_point(aes(subjareas, mean, size = sample)) + 
  theme_linedraw() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust=1), 
        legend.position = "none") + 
  xlab("Discipline Areas") + 
  ylab("Median, Mean, and IQR of Citation Counts") + 
  coord_flip() + 
  theme(text = element_text(size = 16))
ggsave(here("03_manuscript", "figures", "fig2-desc-r1b.jpg"), width = 10, height = 6)
```

### Model Statistics

```{r hyp1b-statistics}
hyp1b_model <- DF2 %>% filter(grepl("hyp1b", model))
# add predictor information
hyp1b_model$predictor <- rep(c("Year", "team_size", "intercept"), nrow(hyp1b_model)/3)
hyp1b_model <- hyp1b_model %>% 
  filter(predictor == "team_size") %>% 
  separate(col = "model", 
           into = c("model", "DV", "subjareas"), 
           extra = "merge",
           sep = "_",
           fill = "right") %>% 
    mutate(DV = factor(DV, 
                     levels = c("CitationCount", "Citation5y"),
                     labels = c("Overall Citations", "Citation 5 Years"))) %>% 
  left_join(hyp1b, by = c("subjareas" = "subjareas", "DV" = "DV"))
hyp1b_model$sample[is.na(hyp1b_model$subjareas)] <- sum(hyp1b_model$sample, na.rm = T)/2
# get CIs effects (df = N - k - 1)
hyp1b_model$critical <- qt(.05/2, hyp1b_model$sample - 2 - 1, lower.tail = F)
hyp1b_model$lower <- hyp1b_model$coef - hyp1b_model$critical*hyp1b_model$se
hyp1b_model$upper <- hyp1b_model$coef + hyp1b_model$critical*hyp1b_model$se
# get CIs R2
hyp1b_model$r2lower <- hyp1b_model$r2upper <- NA
for(i in 1:nrow(hyp1b_model)){
  temp <- ci.R2(R2 = hyp1b_model$r2[i], 
        df.1 = 1, 
        df.2 = hyp1b_model$sample[i] - 2 - 1)
  hyp1b_model$r2lower[i] <- temp$Lower.Conf.Limit.R2
  hyp1b_model$r2upper[i] <- temp$Upper.Conf.Limit.R2
}
```

Team size was used to predict citation count, while controlling for
year, which was different from zero, *b* =
`r hyp1b_model %>% filter(is.na(subjareas)) %>% filter(DV == "Overall Citations") %>% pull(coef)`,
95% CI
[`r hyp1b_model %>% filter(is.na(subjareas)) %>% filter(DV == "Overall Citations") %>% pull(lower)`,
`r hyp1b_model %>% filter(is.na(subjareas)) %>% filter(DV == "Overall Citations") %>% pull(upper)`].
Five year citations had a similar result, *b* =
`r hyp1b_model %>% filter(is.na(subjareas)) %>% filter(DV == "Citation 5 Years") %>% pull(coef)`,
95% CI
[`r hyp1b_model %>% filter(is.na(subjareas)) %>% filter(DV == "Citation 5 Years") %>% pull(lower)`,
`r hyp1b_model %>% filter(is.na(subjareas)) %>% filter(DV == "Citation 5 Years") %>% pull(upper)`].
These results indicated that approximately 10 extra authors were
associated with at least one more citation. The bottom of Figure
\@ref(fig:fig-heatmap) shows the results by subject area. Each subject
area showed a coefficient greater than zero, but the overall effect size
for the physical sciences was not different from zero. Multidisciplinary
and social sciences showed the largest effects and coefficients,
followed by life and health sciences. Each additional team member was
associated with up to two extra citations for research manuscripts. The
coefficients are presented with their 95% confidence interval in
Appendix A.

```{r create-heata}
hyp1a_model_heat <- hyp1a_model %>% 
  filter(!is.na(subjareas)) %>% 
  select(subjareas, coef, lower, upper) %>% 
  mutate(Estimate = "b") %>% 
  bind_rows(
    hyp1a_model %>% 
      filter(!is.na(subjareas)) %>% 
      select(subjareas, r2, r2lower, r2upper) %>% 
      rename(coef = r2, 
             lower = r2lower,
             upper = r2upper) %>% 
      mutate(Estimate = "Effect Size")
  ) %>% 
    mutate(heat_label = ifelse(
    lower < .0001 & upper > .0001, "NS", "")) %>% 
  mutate(Estimate = factor(Estimate, levels = c("Effect Size", "b"))) %>% 
  mutate(DV = "Team Size")

hyp1a_model_heat <- hyp1a_model_heat %>%
  mutate(text_label = ifelse(
    heat_label == "NS",
    paste0("NS\n", sprintf("%.3f", coef)),
    sprintf("%.3f", coef)
  ))

heat_results_a <- ggplot(hyp1a_model_heat, aes(subjareas, Estimate, fill = coef)) + 
  geom_tile(color = "white", lwd = 1.5, linetype = 1) +
  coord_fixed() + 
  scale_y_discrete(labels  = c(TeX("$R^2$"), TeX("$b$"))) + 
  ylab("") + 
  xlab("") + 
  facet_wrap(~DV) + 
  theme_linedraw() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 75, vjust = .50), 
        legend.position = "right", 
        legend.key.size = unit(.75, 'cm')) + 
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Spectral", name = "Estimate") + 
  theme(text = element_text(size = 12)) + 
  geom_text(aes(label = text_label), size = 4) 
  
```

```{r create-heatb}
hyp1b_model_heat <- hyp1b_model %>% 
  filter(!is.na(subjareas)) %>%

    hyp1b_model %>%

hyp1b_model_heat <- hyp1b_model_heat %>%

  ))


heat_results_b <- ggplot(hyp1b_model_heat, aes(subjareas, Estimate, fill = coef)) +

## Research Question 2: What characteristics of team composition have the strongest association with article metrics?

### Model Statistics Overall

Each author variable was added to the previous model of team size and
year predicting citation counts and five-year citation counts. Appendix
A includes the coefficients for each of the author variables and
dependent variable combinations. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-hyp2) displays
both the coefficients and effect sizes for each independent and
dependent variable combination. All coefficients and effect sizes were
different from zero, but the effects were small in practical terms. The
models that included team size, year, and one author variable explained
between 0.4% and 3.5% of the variance in overall citations and between
1.9% and 7.2% of the variance in five-year citations (for reference, team
size and year alone explained 0.1% and 2.1%, respectively), so the
author variables themselves account for even less unique variance. In general, all effects were positive, with one
exception (gender percent). Higher numbers of countries and/or
institutions were associated with higher numbers of citations with a
stronger effect for more countries than institutions. *h*-index
increases for first or last author were associated with more overall
citations. Papers received more citations if the first or last author
was male, but the effect was stronger if the first author was male.
Last, the only negative predictor was the percent of males included on a
manuscript (as compared to female, unknown, and missing values). As the
overall proportion of males increased, the number of citations
was lower. The coefficients indicate that the effects for each of these
variables is stronger (i.e., higher *b* values) for overall citations,
but the effect sizes indicate more variance accounted for when
explaining five-year citation rates.

```{r hyp2-statistics}
hyp2_model <- DF2 %>% filter(grepl("hyp2", model))
hyp2_model$model <- gsub("country_count", "countrycount", hyp2_model$model)
hyp2_model$model <- gsub("inst_count", "instcount", hyp2_model$model)
hyp2_model$model <- gsub("gender_percent", "genderpercent", hyp2_model$model)
hyp2_model$model <- gsub("HIndex_noself", "HIndexnoself", hyp2_model$model)
hyp2_model$model <- gsub("IPG_index", "IPGindex", hyp2_model$model)
# add predictor information
hyp2_model$predictor <- rep(c("Year", "team_size", "author_var", "intercept"), nrow(hyp2_model)/4)
hyp2_model <- hyp2_model %>% 
  filter(predictor == "author_var") %>% 
  separate(col = "model", 
           into = c("model", "DV", "IV", "subjareas"), 
           extra = "merge",
           sep = "_",
           fill = "right") %>% 
    mutate(DV = factor(DV, 
                     levels = c("CitationCount", "Citation5y"),
                     labels = c("Overall Citations", "Citation 5 Years"))) %>% 
  left_join(hyp1b, by = c("subjareas" = "subjareas", "DV" = "DV"))
hyp2_model$sample[is.na(hyp2_model$subjareas)] <- hyp1b_model$sample[is.na(hyp1b_model$subjareas)][1]
# get CIs effects (df = N - k - 1)
hyp2_model$critical <- qt(.05/2, hyp2_model$sample - 2 - 1, lower.tail = F)
hyp2_model$lower <- hyp2_model$coef - hyp2_model$critical*hyp2_model$se
hyp2_model$upper <- hyp2_model$coef + hyp2_model$critical*hyp2_model$se
# get CIs R2
hyp2_model$r2lower <- hyp2_model$r2upper <- NA
for(i in 1:nrow(hyp2_model)){
  temp <- suppressWarnings(ci.R2(R2 = hyp2_model$r2[i], 
        df.1 = 1, 
        df.2 = hyp2_model$sample[i] - 2 - 1))
  hyp2_model$r2lower[i] <- temp$Lower.Conf.Limit.R2
  hyp2_model$r2upper[i] <- temp$Upper.Conf.Limit.R2
}
# mark all the first versus last authors
hyp2_model <- unique(hyp2_model[ , -1]) #drop row.x
hyp2_model <- 
  hyp2_model %>% 
  group_by(DV, IV, subjareas) %>% 
  mutate(author_no = row_number())
```

```{r fig-hyp2, fig.width=10, fig.height=8, fig.cap="Author variable coefficients (top) and effect sizes (bottom) predicting citation counts and five year citation counts. 95% confidence intervals are displayed but are very narrow due to large sample size. Appendix A includes all exact values for reference."}
hyp2_model$IV2 <- paste(hyp2_model$IV, hyp2_model$author_no)
hyp2_model$IV2 <- factor(hyp2_model$IV2,
                         levels = c("countrycount 1", "genderpercent 1", 
                                    "instcount 1", 
                                    "HIndex 1", "HIndex 2", 
                                    "HIndexnoself 1", "HIndexnoself 2",
                                    "IPGindex 1", "IPGindex 2"),
                         labels = c("Country Count", "Gender Percent", 
                                    "Institution Count", "h-Index First",
                                    "h-Index Last", "h-Index No-Self First",
                                    "h-Index No-Self Last", "Gender First", 
                                    "Gender Last"))

coef_hyp2 <- ggplot(hyp2_model %>% filter(is.na(subjareas)), aes(IV2, coef, color = DV )) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin=r2lower, ymax=r2upper)) + 
  theme_linedraw() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 0.5), 
        legend.position = "bottom") + 
  xlab("Author Variable") + 
  ylab("Coefficient") + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + 
  coord_flip() + 
  theme(text = element_text(size = 16)) 

effect_size_hyp2 <- ggplot(hyp2_model %>% filter(is.na(subjareas)), aes(IV2, r2, color = DV )) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin=r2lower, ymax=r2upper)) + 
  theme_linedraw() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 0.5), 
        legend.position = "bottom") + 
  xlab("Author Variable") + 
  ylab("Effect Size") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, .08)) + 
  coord_flip() + 
  theme(text = element_text(size = 16))

coef_hyp2 + effect_size_hyp2 + plot_layout(nrow = 2, guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = 'bottom')

ggsave(here("03_manuscript", "figures", "fig4-coef-effect-r2.jpg"), width = 10, height = 8)
```

Last, these analyses were separated by subject area. Figure
\@ref(fig:fig-hyp2-coef) displays the coefficients, and Figure
\@ref(fig:fig-hyp2-effect) portrays the $R^2$ effect sizes for each
independent and dependent variable combination. All coefficients and
effect sizes were non-zero using our confidence interval criterion.
Appendix A includes exact coefficients and effect sizes for each of the
author variables and dependent variable combinations. We examine
the patterns of interest below.

**Gender**. These results indicate different effects for gender from the
overall statistics. Multidisciplinary statistics for gender are always
negative when examining male versus female first and last authors. This
result indicates that female authors often see higher citation counts
than male authors. The life sciences split into positive and negative -
papers receive more citations, with a female author in last place, while
male authors in the first author slot receive more citations. All other
gender comparisons are positive, resulting in male-authored papers
receiving more citations. Gender percentage is also split between
negative and positive coefficients. The social sciences largely drive
this effect, wherein papers with larger proportions of male authors
receive significantly fewer citations. Health sciences also included
negative gender percent predictions. Interestingly, the physical
sciences showed a negative effect for the proportion of males on
five-year citation rates, but a positive effect on overall citation
rates. The life sciences and multidisciplinary subject areas were both
positive effects.

**Country and Institution**. Higher country and institution counts were both
associated with more citations. These effects were always larger for
the overall citations than the five-year citation counts; however, the
effect sizes were again always larger for five-year citation models than
overall citation models.

**h-index**. The general pattern for *h*-index effects were positive
with larger effects for no-self citations versus including
self-citations and first author versus last author. Multidisciplinary
papers and the social sciences also tended to have the largest increase
in citation counts when authors with higher *h*-indices were included on
a manuscript. These coefficients were generally stronger for overall
citations, but again, the effect sizes were often larger for five-year
citation patterns.

```{r fig-hyp2-effect, fig.width=10, fig.height=8, fig.cap = "Author variable coefficients predicting citation counts and five year citation counts separated by subject area. 95% confidence intervals are displayed but are very narrow due to large sample size. Appendix A includes all exact values for reference."}
cite_count <- 
  ggplot(hyp2_model %>% 
         filter(!is.na(subjareas)), aes(IV2, r2, color = subjareas)) + 
  geom_point() +  
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin=r2lower, ymax=r2upper)) + 
  theme_linedraw() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust=0.5), 
        legend.position = "bottom") + 
  xlab("Author Variable") + 
  ylab("Effect Size") + 
  coord_flip() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") + 
  scale_color_brewer(name = "Subject Areas", palette = "Dark2") +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(DV)) + 
  theme(text = element_text(size = 16))

cite_count

ggsave(here("03_manuscript", "figures", "fig5-subj-effect-r2.jpg"), width = 12, height = 8)
```

# Discussion

## *Question 1*. What is the pattern of team size distribution within various disciplines over time, and is team size related to article impact?

The first research question in this paper addressed the pattern of team
size distribution within various disciplines over time and the
relationship between team size and article impact. Our findings indicate
a consistent increase in team size across disciplines, corroborating
previous research on the expansion of scientific
collaboration [@wuchty2007; @larivière2015]. The trend was most
pronounced in the physical sciences, aligning with reports of a
substantial rise in team sizes in physics and musculoskeletal science
over the past few decades [@russell2019; @nabout2015]. Notably, the
social sciences exhibited the lowest median number of authors per
manuscript, a trend that may reflect long-standing disciplinary norms
favoring single or small team authorship [@henriksen2016].

Similarly, while growth was seen in the social sciences, this discipline
had the lowest median number of authors per manuscript. In psychology,
for example, this may be due to the long periods of solo-author
dominance, followed by a rise in teams of two and, recently teams of
three [at least based on specific journal metrics, @kozlowski2017].
Henriksen [-@henriksen2016] notes that co-authorship has grown in the
social sciences between 1980 and 2013, but the median number of authors
per article remains low relative to other disciplines. Interestingly,
Paul-Hus et al. [-@paul-hus2020] explain that while co-authorship remains
low in the social sciences, when taking acknowledgments into
consideration, the total number of contributors more closely resembles
that found in other disciplines. Looking at authorship and
acknowledgment trends concurrently may represent an important area of
future research that illuminates authorship norms among various
disciplines and guides conversations about crediting. Despite this
variation, the broader increase in co-authorship aligns with the 
necessity of interdisciplinary and large-scale collaborations to address
complex scientific challenges [@samarasekera2009]. These trends may be
influenced by funding opportunities favoring collaborative efforts, the
need for diverse expertise in tackling intricate research questions, and
the growing complexity of modern scientific inquiry.

Our analysis also found a positive association between team size and
article impact, as measured by citation counts, consistent with previous
findings that collaborative works tend to garner more
citations [@thijs2015; @wuchty2007]. These data are observational, and
the association should not be read as team size driving citations. It may
partly reflect characteristics that co-occur with larger teams, such as
disciplines in which both team size and citation counts are high; our
by-discipline analyses show that the association was present within each
of the five broad subject areas, but these areas remain coarse (e.g.,
large-team fields such as particle physics and genomics are grouped with
smaller-team fields), so residual disciplinary differences cannot be ruled
out, and finer-grained disciplinary controls could change the estimates.
One potential explanation for the association is the increased
dissemination of collaborative research through multiple authors'
networks, leading to broader recognition and citation. Larger teams may
also bring more collective expertise, which could improve the robustness
and credibility of findings [@larivière2015], and larger teams have more
opportunities for self-citation, which would inflate citation counts
because our citation outcomes included self-citations. We also did not
account for journal quality (e.g., impact factor, CiteScore, or SJR);
articles in more prestigious journals tend to be cited more, and larger
or more diverse teams may be more likely to publish in such journals, so
journal quality is a plausible confounder of the associations reported
here. While the relationship between team size and citations appears
generally positive, it is not necessarily linear. Prior studies have
suggested that citation benefits plateau beyond a certain threshold (e.g.,
approximately 20 authors), indicating diminishing returns for excessively
large teams [@sharma2021]. We modeled team size as a linear term, so we
could not evaluate this possibility directly. Future research should
explore potential moderators, such as discipline-specific authorship norms
and the role of team leadership in fostering impactful collaborations.

## *Question 2*. What characteristics of team composition have the strongest association with article metrics?

### Gender

Gender composition was associated with citation rates, though the
associations varied by discipline. We caution against interpreting these
patterns as an effect of author gender on citing behavior. Readers
frequently cannot infer authors' gender (e.g., from initials or unfamiliar
names), and researchers generally cite work for its relevance, novelty,
methodological quality, or venue. A more plausible reading is that gender
is correlated with other factors that we did not model, such as career
stage, institutional prestige, funding, journal quality, topic, and
finer-grained disciplinary differences, as well as with disciplinary norms
regarding authorship position, scientific networks, and systemic
inequities in academia. Consistent with prior research, our results
indicate that male-dominated authorship teams tended to receive fewer
citations in social sciences and health sciences, whereas in some
disciplines, particularly the life sciences, male first authors were
associated with higher citation counts [@west2013; @maliniak2013]. Prior
studies that did account for some of these factors have suggested that
gender biases in citation practices may persist, with work authored by
women under-cited in some fields, particularly fields historically
dominated by male researchers [@cameron2016]; our models cannot test that
explanation. Because the gender variable was inferred rather than
self-reported, and because effect sizes were small, these results should
be treated as descriptive.

In the life sciences, papers received more citations when there was a
female author in the last place and male authors in the first spot.
These findings may reflect the various authorship norms for life
sciences subdisciplines, wherein the weight of one’s contributions is
associated with particular authorship positions. In all other instances,
male-authored papers received more citations. This is compatible with previous
research that highlights the systematic devaluation of women’s
peer-reviewed contributions and research that is considered
*feminine* [@ni2021] or that focuses on *women’s issues* [@mirin2021].
Another possible explanation for the observed disparities is the
tendency for women to engage in broader collaboration networks, which
may enhance the visibility of their work [@zeng2016]. However, systemic
barriers, including inequitable crediting of contributions and biases in
authorship order conventions, may still limit women’s perceived
impact [@ross2022]. Moreover, prior research suggests that gender gaps in
citation rates may be exacerbated by self-citation practices, as men are
more likely to cite their previous work, thereby inflating their
citation metrics [@hutson2002]. Because our citation outcomes included
self-citations, this pathway cannot be separated from other explanations
here.

### Institution and Country

Our findings highlight the citation advantages associated with
institutional and geographic diversity. Collaboration across
institutions and national borders was positively associated with
citation counts, consistent with prior studies indicating that international
co-authorship is associated with greater article visibility and impact [@katz1997;
@khor2016]. These associations may not reflect an independent effect of
collaboration. They could instead reflect unmeasured factors, such as
larger grants, participation in international consortia, publication in
higher-impact journals, or institutional prestige, that make both
multi-institution authorship and higher citation counts more likely. Notably,
articles in multidisciplinary journals and collaborations spanning multiple
countries were associated with the highest citation rates. Note that
"multidisciplinary" is a characteristic of the journal, not of the
authorship team, so this result speaks to publication venue rather than to
team composition. The pattern is compatible with the increasing
recognition of global, cross-disciplinary perspectives in addressing
scientific challenges [@coccia2016]. These results are also compatible with
the argument that international collaborations may facilitate access to
diverse expertise and resources, potentially enhancing research quality and
its subsequent impact [@kliegl2011].

Beyond increased citation impact, international collaborations can also
contribute to a more comprehensive and innovative approach to research
questions by integrating diverse methodological perspectives and
theoretical frameworks [@coccia2016a]. The exchange of ideas across
different scientific traditions and institutional structures can lead to
the development of novel insights and more rigorous analytical
approaches [@wang2015]. Additionally, researchers engaged in
international partnerships may benefit from greater access to funding
opportunities, as many governmental and private organizations prioritize
collaborative, multinational research initiatives [@walsh2007]. However,
challenges such as differences in institutional policies, language
barriers, and variations in research infrastructure may also shape the
effectiveness of these collaborations. Future research should examine
how these structural and logistical factors impact collaboration
outcomes and whether specific disciplines are more adept at leveraging
international partnerships for research advancement.

### *h*-Index

The positive association between h-index and citation counts was evident
across all disciplines, with stronger effects observed for last authors
compared to first authors. This finding is compatible with the idea that researchers
with established publication records tend to attract more citations,
potentially due to their reputation and extensive academic
networks [@geraci2015]. Interestingly, the relationship between h-index
and citation count was more pronounced when self-citations were
excluded, which is consistent with, but does not demonstrate, high-impact researchers benefitting from external
validation rather than self-referential practices [@leimu2005]. This
highlights the importance of distinguishing between genuine academic
influence and self-reinforcing citation behaviors when assessing
scholarly impact. Additionally, scholars with higher h-indices may have
greater access to institutional resources, mentorship opportunities, and
visibility in high-impact journals, further compounding their influence
on citation metrics. Future research should explore how variations in
h-index across disciplines and career stages affect long-term scholarly
impact.

The limitations of *h*-index as a universal metric must also be
acknowledged. It does not account for field-specific citation norms, and
early-career researchers and those publishing in niche areas may be at a
disadvantage. In addition, we used the *h*-index of the last author as an
indicator of an experienced author, but authorship conventions differ
across disciplines (e.g., alphabetical ordering or other author-order
practices), so the last author is not necessarily the most senior member of
the team, and the first/last author comparison may be biased in fields
that do not follow the first/last convention. Alternative bibliometric indicators, such as
the i10-index or g-index, may provide complementary insights into
scholarly impact by addressing some of these limitations. Moreover, as
open-access publishing continues to rise, its potential impact on
citation disparities linked to h-index should be explored further.

## Conclusion and Future Directions

In summary, our study documents the growing prominence of scientific
collaboration and its association with citation metrics. Team size and
institutional and international diversity were positively associated with
citation counts, and gender representation also showed varied
associations with citations that differed by discipline. These
associations were small in magnitude: the models explained, at most, about
7% of the variance in citations, and the author variables explained only a
fraction of that. Statistical significance was assured by the size of the
dataset, so the practical size of the effects is what matters for
interpretation.

*Limitations.* The analyses are observational, so the associations cannot
be interpreted causally. We used linear models for count outcomes that
are skewed and heteroscedastic; used five broad subject areas that hide
large differences in collaboration practices within them; did not control
for journal quality, career stage, institutional prestige, or funding; and
included self-citations in the citation outcomes. The *h*-index is a
contested measure, and last-author position is an imperfect proxy for
seniority. Gender was inferred rather than self-reported, and we analyzed
a 25% random sample of eligible articles. Any of these may account for part
of the observed associations.

*Implications.* Given the small effect sizes and the likelihood of
confounding, these findings do not support using team size, team
composition, or author *h*-index as stand-alone indicators in research
evaluation, funding allocation, hiring, or promotion decisions; such uses
risk rewarding correlates of citation counts rather than the quality or
contribution of the work. They are better suited to describing how
collaboration practices differ across fields and to informing institutional
policies that remove barriers to inclusive collaboration (for example,
by supporting cross-institution and international partnerships and by
examining how credit is assigned in teams) without presuming that such
collaboration will in itself raise citation counts.

*Future directions.* Future research should test these relationships with
models suited to count data (e.g., negative binomial), include interactions
among team size, time, and composition variables, add journal-level and
career-stage controls, and use finer-grained subject classifications.
Additionally, exploring the intersectionality of gender, institutional
affiliation, and career stage could provide a more nuanced understanding of
how different factors are jointly related to research visibility and
impact. Finally, the recent adoption of large language models (LLMs) in
research and writing may be changing how researchers collaborate and how
teams are formed, for example by changing the amount of work that can be
done by small teams or by lowering barriers across languages and
disciplines. Whether team sizes and collaboration patterns have shifted
since the widespread availability of LLMs is an empirical question that
our data, which end at the data snapshot date, were not designed to
address; the trends reported here provide a pre-LLM baseline against which
such changes could be evaluated in future team science research. As the
scientific enterprise continues to evolve, ensuring equitable and
inclusive collaboration practices will be essential.
